SAM9X75-Curiosity","content":"# 3.4.10 MIPI CSI/DSI Interface The SAM9X75-Curiosity board embeds a 4-lane MIPI D-PHY for interfacing with CSI compatible cameras and DSI compatible displays. The board features a 22-pin FPC/FFC connector (J29) with 0.5 mm pitch, similar to the one used for the Raspberry Pi Compute Module boards. 4-lane MIPI cameras can connect to the board directly, while 2-lane cameras and displays provided by Raspberry Pi^[(1)](GUID-C898D0DE-85AB-4956-9D37-ECB937CDC470.html#GUID-C898D0DE-85AB-4956-9D37-ECB937CDC470__GUID-A76F9D3F-E9D8-4497-8B37-27260EE18064)^ require a 22-pin to 15-pin FPC adapter. For 4-lane MIPI displays, an adapter is necessary due to various non-standard connector pinout across different manufacturers. Additional GPIOs and TWI interface are provided for camera/display control. Note: 1. Raspberry Pi is a trademark of Raspberry Pi Trading. The following figure shows the MIPI CSI camera interface. The following table shows the MIPI CSI/DSI interface signal description. | Pin No. | PIO | Signal Name | Signal Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19 | \u2013 | GND | Ground | | 2 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D0\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input data 0 | | 3 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D0\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input data 0 | | 5 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D1\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input data 1 | | 6 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D1\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input data 1 | | 8 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_CK\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input clock | | 9 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_CK\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input clock | | 11 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D2\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input data 2 | | 12 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D2\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input data 2 | | 14 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D3\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input data 3 | | 15 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D3\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input data 3 | | 17 | PC19 | MIPI\\_CSI\\_GPIO0 | General Purpose I/O | | 18 | PC15 | MIPI\\_CSI\\_GPIO1 | General Purpose I/O | | 20 | PA25 | CAM\\_I\u00B2C\\_CLK\\_ | TWI Clock | | 21 | PA24 | CAM\\_I\u00B2C\\_DATA | TWI Data | | 22 | \u2013 | VDD\\_3V3 or 5V\\_MAIN | 3.3V or 5V |\\n\\n Images: https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-69CFF0CC-BD83-4DB3-AA72-E309A819F68E-en-US-3/GUID-C363CF13-ABF3-4ECC-A292-836C41C8662A-high.png","url":"https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-69CFF0CC-BD83-4DB3-AA72-E309A819F68E-en-US-3/GUID-C898D0DE-85AB-4956-9D37-ECB937CDC470.html?utm_source=mchpmcp","keywords":["3.4.10 MIPI CSI/DSI Interface - SAM9X75-Curiosity","SAM9X75-Curiosity"],"relevancyScore":48.783096},{"title":"3.4 Peripherals - SAM9X75-Curiosity","content":"# 3.4 Peripherals Several interfaces and connectors are implemented in the SAM9X75-Curiosity board with the purpose of enabling the user to exploit all the features that the MPU can offer and to facilitate a reference design for future customer applications. This section describes the following peripherals mounted on the SAM9X75-Curiosity board: - USB host/device - mikroBUS interface - Controller Area Network (CAN) interface - GPIO interface - Inter-IC Sound Multi-Channel Controller (I2SMCC) interface - Gigabit Ethernet interface - microSD card (Secure Digital Multimedia Card, SDMMC) - Wireless M.2 interface - Video LVDS interface - MIPI camera interface - LCD module positioning over motherboard - Audio Class D","url":"https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-69CFF0CC-BD83-4DB3-AA72-E309A819F68E-en-US-3/GUID-79C1CC89-14B8-47B6-B525-F5D1880775F5.html?utm_source=mchpmcp","keywords":["3.4 Peripherals - SAM9X75-Curiosity","SAM9X75-Curiosity"],"relevancyScore":42.96505},{"title":"SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board - Features","content":"{{OnThisPage depth=\u00223\u0022/}}\n\nThis topic describes the features of the [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board (P/N: EV31H43A)](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/development-tool/EV31H43A) with links to additional information.\n\n## Features Summary\nThe major features of the SAM9X60-EK Evaluation Kit are:\n\n- SAM9X75D2G MPU\n- Mass storage\n- Communications\n- Debugging\n- User interface\n- Expansion\n- Power options\n- Jumper summary\n\n### References\n- [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/introduction/WebHome)\n\n[SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/image:sam9x75d2g/png)\n\n## SAM9X75D2G MPU\nThe [SAM9X75D2G](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/product/SAM9X75D2G) System-in-Package (SiP) is a high-performance, ultra-low-power ARM926EJ-S\u2122 Arm\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E Thumb\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E CPU-based embedded microprocessor (MPU) running up to 800 MHz, with a 2 Gbit integrated DDR3L memory. Its features include:\n\n- 800 MHz ARM926EJ-S Core, 266 MHz System/Memory Bus\n- 2 Gbit integrated DDR3L Memory\n- 64 kB internal SRAM\n- MIPI Display Serial Interface (MIPI DSI\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E) and LVDS display interface\n- 2D graphics processor unit\n- MIPI-CSI-2 Camera interface\n- A Gigabit Ethernet interface through SODIMM 260-pin connector\n- Dual Control Area Network (CAN)\n- One microSD card interface, One M.2 Key E connector/radio module interface\n- One Micro-B USB device, two USB Type-A connectors\n- Thirteen FLEXCOMs (Universal Synchronous Asynchronous Receiver Transmitter (USART), Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI), and Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C))\n- Hardware encryption engine and True Random Number Generator (TRNG)\n- Secure boot\n\n## Mass Storage\nThere are three mass storage options available on the development board.\n\n### 4 Gb NAND Flash (U5)\nU3 is a 4 Gb (512M x 8) NAND Flash memory ([Macronix](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/macronix/com/en-us/Pages/default/aspx) MX30LF4G28AD-XKI). It is connected to the NAND Flash controller of the SAM9X75D2G.\n\n### 64 Mb Serial Quad I/O (SQI) Flash Device with EUI-48 and EUI-64 (U6)\nU6 is a 64 Mb Serial Quad I/O\u2122 (SQI\u2122) flash device with EUI-48 and EUI-64 memory ([Microchip SST26VF064BEUI](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/microchip/com/en-us/product/sst26vf064beui)). It is connected to the Quad SPI Interface peripheral of the SAM9x75D2G.\n\n### Micro Secure Digital (J14)\nJ14 is a microSD memory card slot. It is connected to the Secure Digital MultiMediaCard port 0 (SDMMC0) peripheral of the SAM9X75D2G.\n\n![sam9x75 Curiosity Mass Storage](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/download/attachments/sam9x75_massstorage.png)\n\n## Communications\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board provides wired communications via Ethernet, USB, and CAN.\n\n![sam9x75 Curiosity Mass Storage](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/download/attachments/peripherals.png)\n\n### Ethernet (J17)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board features a Gigabit Ethernet interface through a SODIMM 260-pin connector. The SAM9X75 Curiosity LAN kit comes with a [LAN8840 EDS2 daughter card](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/development-tool/ev12n54a) to evaluate the Microchip LAN8840 Gigabit Ethernet RGMII Ethernet PHYOne Gigabit Ethernet interface through the SODIMM 260-pin connector.\n\n### CAN Interface\nThe SAM9X75-Curiosity board shares the CAN interface with the UART signals of the mikroBUS\u2122 connector (J25). Use the mikroBUS Click MIKROE-2299 that embeds a Microchip MCP2542WFD to connect the SAM9X75 Curiosity to a CAN.\n\n### USB (J2, J15 and J16)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board features three USB communication ports (J2 - USB 2.0 Micro-B (USB-A), J15 - USB Type-A (USB-B), J16 - USB Type-A (USB-C)).\n\nThe USB-A port acts only as a USB device interface and is accessed via USB Micro-B connector J7.\n\n\u003E Note: The USB-A port (J2) is used as a power source for the development board.\n\n\u003E Note: The USB-A port (J2) is used as the default serial port used to communicate with the [SAM-BA\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E monitor](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/programmers-and-debuggers/32-bit-isp/monitor/WebHome) resident on the MPU.\n\nThe USB-B and USB-C ports are connected to the stacked USB Type-A connecter (J15 \u0026 J16). Each port can act both as a device and as a host.\n\n### Wireless M.2 interface (J20)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity board embeds an M.2 connector to interconnect with wireless modules. M.2 (formerly known as NGFF) is a small form factor card and connector that supports applications such as Wi-Fi\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E, WLAN, USB, PCIe\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E and SATA, as defined in the PCI-SIG\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E M.2 Specification. The default interface used with the wireless module solution is the SDIO. However, the wireless module can be controlled in SPI mode and configuration can be performed manually by the end user. The interface is based on a 67-pin connector and includes a clock, SDIO/SPI interface, USART Interface, wake-up/interrupt, reset, and power lines.\n\n## Debugging\nThere is one method of debugging the SAM9X75 Curiosity Development board via JTAG. In addition, a console serial communication port (J11) is available for debugging.\n\n### JTAG (J34)\nA JTAG interface to the SAM9X75-Curiosity is provided by 20-pin connector J34. This facilitates software development and debugging by connecting an external JTAG debugger such as the [MPLAB\u00AE PICkit\u2122 5 In-Circuit Debugger](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/microchip/com/en-us/development-tool/pg164150) or [J-32 Debug Probe](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/microchip/com/en-us/development-tool/DV164232).\n\n\u003E Alert: The JTAG interface signals voltage levels are 3.3V.\n\n### Serial UART Debug Port (J35)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board features a dedicated serial UART port (J35) (3.3 VDC TTL level) for communicating with the target console.\n\n{{info}}\nNote: For more information, see the \u0022//[SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board - Console Serial Communications](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/console-serial-communications/WebHome)//\u0022 page.\n{{/info}}\n\n## User Interface\n### Red-Green-Blue (RGB) LED (LD1)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board features one RGB LED (LD1).\n\n### Pushbuttons (SW1-SW4)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board contains four push buttons:\n\n- USER (SW1): User push button which is available for user\u2019s usage\n- WKUP (SW2): Will wake up the processor when it has been shut down by software\n- RESET (SW3): Reset push button, when pressed the system resets\n- START (SW4): When pressed, the PMIC start-up sequence is initiated if the buck converters are off\n\n### LCD Interface (J28, J29)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board contains both LVDS display interface(J28) and MIPI display serial interface(J29).\n\nCompatible Microchip LCD modules (LVDS Display [AC69T88A](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/development-tool/AC69T88A)  and MIPI DSI [AC40T08A](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/development-tool/ac40t08a) ) can be connected to the SAM9X75 Curiosity board.\n\n### MIPI CSI/DSI (J29)\nThe SAM9X75-Curiosity board embeds a 4-lane MIPI D-PHY for interfacing with CSI-compatible cameras and DSI-compatible displays.\n\n## Expansion\n### mikroBUS\u2122 (25)\nThe [mikroBUS](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/mikroe/com/mikrobus) socket is a proprietary communication and plugin standard for small interface boards called [Click boards\u2122](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/mikroe/com/click) that extends the capabilities of the development board by offering SPI, UART, TWI, and PWM-based sensors and devices. They are made by [MikroElektronika](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/mikroe/com/click), a producer and retailer of hardware and software tools for developing embedded systems.\n\n### GPIO/Raspberry Pi Connector(J27)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board contains a 40-pin GPIO connector (J27) for use. This connector is compatible with the Raspberry Pi expansion header.\n\n## Power Options\nTwo options are available to power up the SAM9X75-Curiosity board, powering through the jack connector (J1) or powering through the USB Micro-B connector on the USBA port (J2).\n\n## Jumper Summary\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board has 9 jumpers. Refer to Section 2.5 of the \u0022//[SAM9X75 Curiosity User Guide](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/aemDocuments/documents/MPU32/ProductDocuments/UserGuides/SAM9X75-Curiosity-User-Guide-DS60001859.pdf)//\u0022 for default jumper settings.\n\n## Learn More\n- [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board \u2013 Introduction](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/introduction/WebHome)\n- [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board \u2013 Console Serial Port](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/console-serial-communications/WebHome)\n- [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board \u2013 Booting Demo Linux\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E Image](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/booting-demo-linux-image/WebHome)\n- [Developing with Embedded Linux](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/linux/WebHome)\n- [Developing Applications with MPLAB Harmony 3 Software Framework for MPUs](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/32-bit-harmony-v3/WebHome)","url":"https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/features/?utm_source=mchpmcp","keywords":["SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board - Features"],"relevancyScore":49.707714}]},"timestamp":"2026-05-02T16:29:37Z"}

4. Errors and fixes:
   - **PHY_FATAL=0x3 SOT sync errors at 972 Mbps with HSFREQRANGE=0x1A**: SAM9X75 is DWC Gen3 per DT snps,phy_type=<0>. Fixed by changing ISC_CAP_CSI_BITRATE from 0x1A (Gen2 value) to 0x0A (Gen3 value for 950-1000 Mbps band).
   
   - **180-row cliff with PACKED8**: PFE_CFG1/2 were reset-zero (MCC never calls ISC_PFE_Crop_Area). Partially fixed by writing crop + COLEN/ROWEN. But cliff persisted at 180 rows × 3840 bytes = 691,200 bytes/frame due to ISC treating CSI2DC's 32-bit VP output words as 1-byte samples.
   
   - **ISC_Update_Profile hang**: UPPRO never clears when capture isn't running. Reverted the call. User feedback was to revert.
   
   - **Bandwidth contention hypothesis wrong**: User said "I don't believe that it's bandwidth limited". LCDC removed from MCC, cliff unchanged. User was correct.
   
   - **Probe hang on BPP change**: When imageWidth was changed to 3840, probe's frame_size calc = 8.3 MB overran 2.7 MB buffer. Fixed by keeping imageWidth at pixel count, only overriding COLMAX.
   
   - **PACKED32 + BPS=EIGHT = sparse memory with bit-spread (12 bytes/pixel)**: Fixed by BPS=FORTY (DRV_IMAGE_SENSOR_40_BIT) → dense 3-byte BGR.
   
   - **ARGB32 RLP mode failed**: 3 different shifted copies of 0xF80 per 12-byte cycle. Cliff at 540 rows. Confirms Phase 5a finding that ARGB32 RLP needs upstream demosaic pipeline. Reverted.

The MPUs offer advanced security functions, like tamper detection, secure boot, secure key storage, TRNG, PUF as well as higher-performance crypto accelerators for AES and SHA. The SAM9X75 series is supported by Microchip\u0027s Mainline Linux distribution as well as Microchip MPLAB Harmony development tools for bare-metal/RTOS support. SAM9X75 is well-suited for industrial and medical applications with or w/o graphical displays up to 1024 x 768, as well as home automation and security system gateways including access control with biometrics. Microchip offers for different supply configurations, fully tested power management solutions respecting the SAM9X75 power sequencing specifications that are referenced in the product specification.\n\n## SAM9X75 Features\n\nLow System Cost and High Value Integration:- 800MHz ARM926EJ-S Core, 266MHz System/Memory Bus\n\nMemories:- 32 KB Data Cache and 32 KB Instruction Cache\n- 64 KB internal SRAM\n- 16-bit DDR databus\n\nEnhanced User Interface capability:- 24-bit LCD Controller with overlays up to 1024 x 768 resolution\n- 2D Graphics Engine\n- LVDS Display Interface\n- RGB 24-bit display interface\n- MIPI-DSI Display interface\n\nCamera Support- Parallel Port\n- MIPI CSI-2 Camera interface\n\nBuilt-in Class D Amplifier\n\nLarge number of connectivity options:- Single 10/100/1G Ethernet\n- One Quad/Octal SPI controller\n- Thirteen FLEXCOMs (USART, SPI and TWI/I2C)\n- Two High-speed USB Host \u002B One High-speed Host or Device\n\nFully-Integrated Security:- Secure Boot with on-chip Secure Key Storage (OTP)\n- Hardware Encryption Engine (TDES, AES and SHA), True Random Generator (TRNG), PUF\n- Physical protection against tamper, 8 tamper detection pins\n- On the Fly scrambling / unscrambling for memories\n\nRich Development Ecosystem:- Free mainline Linux\u00AE Distribution\n- MPLAB\u00AE X Integrated Development Environment and MPLAB\u00AE Harmony v3\n- Multiple Third-party Software and Hardware Solutions\n\nOptimized for Easy PCB Design and Low EMI- TFBGA240, 11x11, 0.65 mm pitch - de-populated ball-out\n- TFBGA256, 9x9, 0.5 mm pitch - de-populated The sole reference documents for product information on SAM9X7 Series microprocessors and DDR2/DDR3L SDRAM memories are listed in Reference Documents.\nIntroduction\nThe SAM9X75 SiP integrates the ARM926 Arm\u00AE processor-based SAM9X75 MPU with an up to 2-Gbit DDR SDRAM. By combining the SAM9X75 with a DDR SDRAM in a single package, PCB routing complexity, area and number of layers are reduced in the majority of cases. This makes board design easier and more robust by facilitating design for EMI, ESD and signal integrity.\nThe SAM9X75 SiP is available in three pin-to-pin compatible SDRAM memory types and densities:\n\u2022 512-Mbit DDR2 SDRAM\n\u2022 1-Gbit DDR3L SDRAM\n\u2022 2-Gbit DDR3L SDRAM\nReference Documents\nType\tName\tAvailable\tLiterature No.\nData sheet\tSAM9X7 Series\twww.microchip.com\tDS60001813\nData sheet\t8M \u00D7 4 BANKS \u00D7 16 BIT DDR2 SDRAM (512 Mbits)\twww.winbond.com\tW9751G6NB\nData sheet\t8M \u00D7 8 BANKS \u00D7 16 BIT DDR3L SDRAM (1 Gbit)\twww.winbond.com\tW631GU6NB\nData sheet\t16M \u00D7 8 BANKS \u00D7 16 BIT DDR3L SDRAM (2 Gbits)\twww.winbond.com\tW632GU6NB\nData Sheet\n\u00A9 2024 Microchip Technology Inc. and its subsidiaries\nDS60001827C - 1","url":"https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/aemDocuments/documents/MPU32/ProductDocuments/DataSheets/SAM9X75-SIP-Series-Data-Sheet-DS60001827.pdf?utm_source=mchpmcp#page=1","keywords":["SAM9X75 SiP Data Sheet","SAM9X75D5M","SAM9X75D5MN0","page1.md"],"relevancyScore":48.576714},{"title":"1.4.1.5 MPU Bootloader Memory Layout - MPLAB\u00AE Harmony 3 Bootloader Library","content":"# 1.4.1.5 MPU Bootloader Memory Layout **MPU Bootloader Persistent Storage Layout** **For SD/eMMC media** - The SD/eMMC media uses FAT-FS file system to store the Bootloader, Application and AT91bootstrap images. **For NAND/Serial Flash media** The placement of the AT91bootstrap, Bootloader and the application in Flash memory should be such that the application will not overwrite the Bootloader/AT91bootstrap, and the Bootloader can properly program the application when it is downloaded. - The application code can be placed anywhere after the bootloader end address. The application start address should be **aligned to Erase Unit Size of the device**. - As the Bootloader code requires the application start address to be mentioned at compile time, it should match in both the application and bootloader - Got it. Your datasheet quote is the key:
- ISC RLP **must** be BYPASS for MIPI RMS (we already have that — correct).
- CSI2DC `DEMUX_DATA[39:24]=0`, `[23:16]=R`, `[15:8]=G`, `[7:0]=B` — so the upper 16 bits are already zero-padded by CSI2DC, and the lower 32 bits are `00 R G B`.

That means if the ISC wrote the full 32-bit RLP sample as-is to DDR, a little-endian read of that 32-bit word gives us `B G R 00` in memory — which is BGRX8888. No conversion needed; it's essentially free.

The reason we aren't seeing that today is that with our current config (`BPS=FORTY + PACKED8 + PACKED32 DCFG + COLMAX=W*3/4-1`) the ISC is pulling 3 packed bytes per pixel (`B G R`), dropping the zero byte. We're telling it there are only `(W*3)/4` 32-bit samples per row, so it compacts 4 pixels into 12 bytes.

To get BGRX32 (4 B/pixel with the alpha/pad byte), we need the ISC to store one 32-bit sample per pixel, i.e.:
- `COLMAX = width - 1` (1280 samples/row, not 960)
- `IMODE = PACKED32` keeps 4 bytes/sample
- `ISC_CAP_BPP = 4`
- Frame size = 1280 × 720 × 4 = 3,686,400 bytes

Before I just try it, I want to confirm one thing from your datasheet. Could you paste (or grep / open locally) the ISC sections on:
1. **PFE_CFG0.BPS** — all enum values and what "samples per line" means in RMS vs non-RMS mode.
2. **DCFG.IMODE** (PACKED8 / PACKED16 / PACKED32) — specifically how many bytes/pixel each stores when RLP=BYPASS.
3. Any register that controls "RMS pixel width" or "RMS sample size" — something that tells the DMA "1 sample per pixel" vs "3 samples per pixel".

If you have the PDF locally I can Read it directly — that'll be faster than me asking piecemeal. What path is it at?

67403	
67404	The Parallel Front End module performs data resampling across clock domain boundary. It includes
67405	a CCIR656 decoder used to convert a standard ITU-R BT.656 stream to 24-bit digital video. It also
67406	generates pixels, syncs flags and valid signals to the main video pipeline. It ouputs field, video
67407	and synchronization signals. The PFE can optionally crop and limit the incoming pixel stream to a
67408	predefined horizontal and vertical value. By default, the PFE only relies on the input horizontal and
67409	vertical references to sample the incoming pixel stream. A pixel is sampled if, and only if, the vertical
67410	and horizontal synchronizations are valid and a pixel clock edge is detected. ISC_PFE_CFG0.BPS
67411	shows the number of bits per sample.
67412	When operating with a parallel interface, the PFE module outputs a 12-bit data on the vp_data[11:0]
67413	bus, and asserts the vp_valid signal when the data can be sampled.

67433	When operating with MIPI RGB or YUV formats, the PFE module copies up to 40-bit data from
67434	isc_data[39:0] bus on the vp_data[39:0] bus, and asserts the vp_valid signal when the data can be
67435	sampled.
67436	The PFE module also includes logic to synchronize capture request with the incoming pixel

67554	50.6.7. Defective Pixel Correction (DPC)
67555	        The ISC can detect and correct defective pixels on Raw Bayer formats up to 12-bit width. The
67556	        defective pixel correction is enabled by writing '1' to ISC_DPC_CTRL.DPCEN.
67557	        The color filter array pattern of the image sensor driven by ISC must be configured in
67558	        ISC_DPC_CFG.BAYCFG.
67559	        It is possible to adjust the processing performed by the defective pixel correction logic.
67560	        Several criteria can be activated to determine if a pixel is defective (edge interpolation, median
67561	        threshold, closest pixel, average threshold).
67562	        The edge interpolation is enabled by writing ISC_DPC_CFG.EITPOL=1.
67563	        The median threshold is enabled by writing ISC_DPC_CFG.TM_ENABLE=1.
67564	        The closest pixel threshold is enabled by writing ISC_DPC_CFG.TC_ENABLE=1.
67565	        The average threshold is enabled by writing ISC_DPC_CFG.TA_ENABLE=1.
67566	        The different thresholds can be configured in ISC_DPC_THRESHM.THRESHM,
67567	        ISC_DPC_THRESHC.THRESHC, ISC_DPC_THRESHA.THRESHA.
67568	        The triggering of a pixel correction can be triggered when all active criteria are met or only one is
67569	        met by configuring the bit ISC_DPC_CFG.ND_MODE.
67570	        The number of corrected pixels by frame are reported in ISC_DPC_SR.COUNTER.
67571	
67572	50.6.8. Green Disparity Correction (GDC)
67573	        The color filter array pattern alternates horizontal lines made of green and blue pixels with lines

68426	50.6.20. DMA Interface
68427	        The descriptor-based DMA interface supports multiple buffers. A DMA stride value shows the offset
68428	        between two consecutive lines (in bytes). If the stride is set to zero, the frame buffer is contiguous.
68429	        When ISC_DCTRL.WB is set (Write Back), the DMA interface performs a single write operation to
68430	        ISC_DCTRL, and sets ISC_DCTRL.DONE to one and ISC_DCTRL.FIELD to the value of the frame field
68431	        when interlaced content is being used. This means that interlaced fields are tagged with their
68432	        relevant field values. The Write Back operation is always performed when the whole frame has been
68433	        transferred to memory.

68577	50.6.21. Histogram Module
68578	             For each possible pixel value, the histogram counts the number of times the value was encountered
68579	             in the current image. RGGB Bayer, raw data or luminance histogram are available. There are
68580	             512 entries in the histogram entries, and each histogram bin can count up to 220 data. As
68581	             the table entries are limited, each bin is actually a range, i.e., least significant bits are ignored.
68582	             A write to ISC_CTRLEN.HISREQ initiates a new histogram. The counting operation ends when
68583	             ISC_INTSR.HISDONE is set. At that time, a software or hardware DMA transfer copies the table from
68584	             the interface to the internal or external memory. To clear the table content (for a new operation),
68585	             use ISC_CTRLEN.HISCLR. An automatic clear (reset after read) is available when ISC_HIS_CFG.RAR is
68586	             set. In that case, as soon as the data is read from the table, the table entry is cleared.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 16:50:43Z)**_

Here's what sections 48–50 actually say, and why we were stuck.

## The failure mode we saw (ARGB32 RLP, mangled colors)

Section 50.6.19 Table (RGB32 RLP mode) expects:
```
rlp_data[31:24] = A = ALPHA[7:0]       (from ISC_RLP_CFG.ALPHA)
rlp_data[23:16] = R = sub420_data[29:22]
rlp_data[15:8]  = G = sub420_data[19:12]
rlp_data[7:0]   = B = sub420_data[9:2]
```

Those bit ranges come from the **CSC module output**, not from raw MIPI. For MIPI RGB888 bypass, the data bus has R at [23:16], G at [15:8], B at [7:0] — a 6/4/2-bit misalignment from what ARGB32 RLP wants. So ARGB32 RLP **cannot** be used when the ISC pipeline is in MIPI bypass. That's structural, not a config mistake.

## Why we currently get dense 3 B/pixel (RMS=1)

Section 49.6.54 VPCFGR.RMS:
- **RMS=0** — "CSI2DC outputs **1 pixel per component per clock cycle**, compliant with the ISC processing engine."
- **RMS=1** — "CSI2DC generates a **byte stream** compliant with the CSI-2 specification memory format."

Our `plib_csi2dc.c:78` hard-codes `CSI2DC_VPCFGR_RMS_1`. Table 49.27 confirms RMS=1 packs 4 BGR pixels into 12 bytes (`B2 R1 G1 B1 | G3 B3 R2 G2 | R4 G4 B4 R3` …). That's exactly our dense output.

## The fix: flip to RMS=0, one pixel per 40-bit VP word

In RMS=0, CSI2DC outputs per Table 49.25:
```
demux_data[39:24] = 0
demux_data[23:16] = R
demux_data[15:8]  = G
demux_data[7:0]   = B
```

Then:
- **RLP = BYPASS** (Mode 15): "32-bit input is sampled and written to the rlp output port. Select this mode for MIPI RMS mode." → `rlp_data[31:0] = demux_data[31:0] = 0x00RRGGBB`
- **DCFG.IMODE = PACKED32**: writes `rlp_data[31:0]` as 4 bytes to memory
- **BPS = FORTY**: 40-bit MIPI input (unchanged)
- **COLMAX = W-1** (1279, not 959)
- **ISC_CAP_BPP = 4**

Little-endian store of `0x00RRGGBB` gives memory bytes `B G R 00` — that's **BGRX32**, what the LCDC expects on the BGRX format. The X byte is 0x00, not 0xFF, but for display-only framebuffers that's fine (alpha ignored). If alpha actually needs to be 0xFF, a cheap CPU pass or `memset32` at buffer init can OR it in.

## Answer to "can it be done in the pipeline?"

**Yes — partially.** RMS=0 + BYPASS + PACKED32 gives BGRX32 with alpha=0x00 for free (no CPU), at the cost of 33% more bandwidth (3.69 MB/frame vs 2.76 MB at 720p60). Setting alpha=0xFF is **not** achievable in-pipeline for MIPI bypass — that requires the CSC module, which is for Bayer/YCbCr.

AI Overview               Mapping 3 bytes to 4 bytes using Direct Memory Access (DMA) on the SAM9X75 (ARM926EJ-S) involves configuring the DMA controller to handle a data size conversion, likely packing 24-bit data (3 bytes) into 32-bit (4 bytes) words in memory.Key Considerations for SAM9X75DMA Controller (XDMAC): The SAM9X75 uses the High-Performance Extended DMA Controller (XDMAC).Data Size: The XDMAC allows independent configuration of the source and destination data widths.Alignment: 4-byte (word) aligned transfers are generally required for optimal performance, meaning the destination buffer must be 32-bit aligned.DMA Configuration StrategyTo transform 3 bytes (\(24\text{ bits}\)) to 4 bytes (\(32\text{ bits}\)), you should configure the XDMAC channel parameters for a "packed" transfer:Source Settings (Peripheral/Memory):Data Width: BYTE (8 bits) or HALFWORD (16 bits).Increment: Yes.Destination Settings (Memory/Peripheral):Data Width: WORD (32 bits).Increment: Yes.The XDMAC controller will then automatically pack the incoming bytes into a single 32-bit word before writing to the destination memory.Implementation Example (Conceptual)You will need to set up the XDMAC_CC_x (Channel Control Register) to enable this packing.c/* Example Conceptual Configuration */
XDMAC->XDMAC_CHID[ch].XDMAC_CC =
    XDMAC_CC_TYPE_PER_TRAN |         // Peripheral to Memory
    XDMAC_CC_SAM_INCREMENTED_AM |    // Source Address Incremented
    XDMAC_CC_DAM_INCREMENTED_AM |    // Dest Address Incremented
    XDMAC_CC_MEMSET_NORMAL |
    XDMAC_CC_DSYNC_PER2MEM |
    XDMAC_CC_CSIZE_CHK_1 |           // Chunk Size
    XDMAC_CC_DWIDTH_WORD |           // Destination width: 32 bits (4 bytes)
    XDMAC_CC_SIF_AHB_IF0 |           // Source Interface
    XDMAC_CC_DIF_AHB_IF1;            // Destination Interface

/* Number of 32-bit words to transfer */
XDMAC->XDMAC_CHID[ch].XDMAC_CUBC = num_32bit_words; 
Use code with caution.Potential PitfallsMisaligned Destination: If the destination address is not 32-bit aligned, the DMA transfer will cause a bus error.Byte Ordering (Endianness): Ensure that the 4-byte mapping corresponds to the expected Little-Endian format of the ARM926EJ-S core.For further details, refer to the SAM9X7 Series Data Sheet  section on XDMAC or utilize the example code provided in the MPLAB Harmony v3 framework.

518	## Session log
519	
520	### 2026-05-02 — 720p60 full-frame capture WORKING; memory format reverse-engineered
521	
522	Huge progress day. Pi as stable 720p60 source, worked through a chain of ISC config issues, ended with full 720-row capture at 60 fps with a deterministic (if quirky) memory layout.
523	
524	**Issues resolved (in order):**
525	
526	1. **PFE crop window never set** (MCC bug). `plib_isc.c` defines `ISC_PFE_Crop_Area()` but nobody calls it. `PFE_CFG1/2` stayed at reset value 0, PFE expected 1×1 frame, fired HDTO on first real line. Fix: write crop directly, AND set COLEN+ROWEN bits in PFE_CFG0 (per Linux mchp-isc driver) to activate.
527	
528	2. **Cliff at 180 rows × 3840 bytes = 691,200 bytes per frame.** Ruled out: LCDC/AHB contention (LCDC removed — no change), burst size (YMBSIZE SINGLE vs BEATS32 — no change), VPCFGR.PA (no change). Diagnostic register dump showed `CSI2DC VPCOL=960 = WC/4`: CSI2DC VP emits 32-bit words to ISC. IMODE=PACKED8 was treating each word as a 1-byte sample → 960 samples/row × 720 rows = 691,200 bytes = the exact cliff.
529	
530	3. **Fix: IMODE=PACKED32.** ISC now writes 4 bytes per CSI2DC word × 960 × 720 = 2,764,800 bytes = full frame. `DCFG=0x00000442`. **60 fps sustained, full 720 rows written per frame.**
531	
532	**Memory layout decoded** (with R/G/B/white/black solid-color tests from Pi):
533	
534	Each pixel occupies **12 bytes**. Channel order is **BGR**. Each 8-bit source byte becomes a 12-bit MSB-aligned value in memory (`0xFF` source → `0xEF0` stored — bridge subtracts 16 from full-range bytes without scaling, so decoded 8-bit equivalent is `0xEF`=239 for `0xFF` input).
535	
536	```
537	Pixel at offset N*12:
538	  +0  B low 8 bits      +4  G low 8 bits      +8  R low 8 bits
539	  +1  G high 4 bits     +5  R high 4 bits     +9  B high 4 bits
540	  +2  0 (pad)           +6  0                 +10 0
541	  +3  0                 +7  0                 +11 0
542	
543	Reconstruction:
544	  B12 = mem[+0] | (mem[+9] << 8);   B8 = B12 >> 4;
545	  G12 = mem[+4] | (mem[+1] << 8);   G8 = G12 >> 4;
546	  R12 = mem[+8] | (mem[+5] << 8);   R8 = R12 >> 4;
547	```
548	
549	Quirk: each channel's high 4 bits land in the chunk BEFORE its own (Blue high → Red chunk, Green high → Blue chunk, Red high → Green chunk), a CSI2DC/ISC streaming artifact. Consistent and decodable.
550	
551	**Data density consequence**: 12 bytes per pixel × 1280 × 720 = 11,059,200 bytes needed for full-resolution; framebuffer holds 2,764,800 bytes. So effective capture is **1/4 horizontal resolution (320 unique pixels × 720 rows)**. On solid colors this is invisible. On real images it's 4:1 horizontal downsampling.
552	
553	**Remaining / carry-forward:**
554	- HDTO bit still fires in INTSR — harmless (informational only; not a stop signal).
555	- 1/4 horizontal resolution — either accept & decode in software (320×720 plenty for guitar fretboard), OR find CSI2DC VP config that emits denser source bytes per output word.
556	- Byte-value range offset: 0xFF → 0xEF. Recoverable via `out = min(255, in + 16)` if needed.
557	
558	**Code state at end of day:**
559	- `isc_capture.c`: PFE crop + COLEN/ROWEN activate; DCFG override to PACKED32 + BEATS32 + CMBSIZE_BEATS32; `csi2dcObj->videoPipeAlign = false` (PA=0); redundant `DRV_ISC_Configure_DMA` call removed.
560	- LCDC removed from MCC config (no contention concerns).
561	- ISC 60fps sustained, full 720-row frames landing in DDR.
562	
563	### 2026-05-01 — Branch `720p`: cliff root-caused to PFE crop; fix applied but unverified
564	
565	**Diagnostic breakthrough**: expanded ISC_Capture_ProbeFrame with a `cliff:` block that reads PFE crop window, ISC DMA state, per-probe CSI2DC/ISC counter deltas, and decoded INTSR error bits. First flash pinpointed the problem:
566	
567	```
568	cliff: PFE_CFG1=0x00000000 PFE_CFG2=0x00000000
569	cliff: PFE crop col[0..0] row[0..0]  expected col[0..1279] row[0..719]
570	cliff: INTSR=0x08000002 [HD HDTO!]
571	cliff: iscObj frameCount=1
572	```
573	
574	**MCC's ISC driver never programs the PFE crop window.** `plib_isc.c` defines `ISC_PFE_Crop_Area()` but nothing calls it, so `PFE_CFG1/2` stay at reset value 0 → PFE expects a 1×1 frame → HDTO (Horizontal Detection Timeout) fires after the first line → ISC halts, no DDONE. This has almost certainly been happening on the 480p path too, but at 480p the bridge drops so many lines that the cliff overlapped with the bridge shortfall.
575	
576	**Fix attempt 1**: program `PFE_CFG1 = COLMAX(w-1)` and `PFE_CFG2 = ROWMAX(h-1)` in `ISC_Capture_Configure` after `DRV_ISC_Configure`. Result: HDTO gone (`INTSR=0x00000002 [HD]` only) — but VD also stopped firing entirely (`frameCount=0` vs `=1` pre-fix). Partial memory writes, no DDONE.
577
```

# marvin HDMI → BGRX32 Capture Pipeline

Authoritative configuration reference for the 720p60 HDMI capture path on SAM9X75. Every stage, every register bit that matters, with datasheet citations. When something breaks, start here before grepping code.

**Status:** working as of 2026-05-02. 1280×720 @ 60 fps, native BGRX32 in DDR, no CPU post-processing.

Datasheet references are to **SAM9X7 Series DS60001813** (sections 48 = MIPI CSI / D-PHY, 49 = CSI2DC, 50 = ISC). TC358743 refs are to the Toshiba datasheet + mainline Linux `drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c`.

---

## 1. Pipeline overview

\```
HDMI source (Pi 720p60 RGB)
        │
        ▼
TC358743 HDMI-to-CSI-2 bridge
  DT=0x24 RGB888, 2 lanes, 972 Mbps/lane, continuous-clock mode
        │
        ▼                          <── MIPI CSI-2 D-PHY
SAM9X75 DWC D-PHY RX Gen3
  HSFREQRANGE=0x0A (950–1000 Mbps band)
        │
        ▼                          <── 40-bit isc_data bus
CSI2DC (Demultiplexer Controller)
  VPCFGR: DT=0x24, VC=0, PA=0, RMS=0
  → demux_data = 0x00_00RRGGBB, one pixel per VP word
        │
        ▼                          <── 40-bit vp_data bus
ISC — Parallel Front End (PFE)
  PFE_CFG0: MIPI=1, BPS=FORTY, MODE=PROGRESSIVE, CONT=1, COLEN=1, ROWEN=1
  PFE_CFG1: COLMIN=0, COLMAX=W-1   (1279)
  PFE_CFG2: ROWMIN=0, ROWMAX=H-1   (719)
        │
        ▼                          <── sub420_data[39:0] (unmodified through ISC)
ISC — Rounding/Limiting/Packing (RLP)
  RLP_CFG: MODE=BYPASS (15)
  → rlp_data[31:0] = sub420_data[31:0] = 0x00RRGGBB
        │
        ▼                          <── rlp_data[31:0]
ISC — DMA Host
  DCFG: IMODE=PACKED32, YMBSIZE=BEATS32, CMBSIZE=BEATS32
  → stores 32-bit words to DDR; little-endian = B G R 00 = BGRX32
        │
        ▼
DDR3 framebuffer  (1280 × 720 × 4 = 3,686,400 B/frame)
  B G R 00  B G R 00  B G R 00  ...
\```

---

## 2. Stage-by-stage configuration

### 2.1 HDMI source

- 1280×720p @ 60 Hz, RGB (not YCbCr), progressive.
- Any stable DVI/HDMI source works. Raspberry Pi with `/boot/firmware/config.txt` forced to `hdmi_group=1 hdmi_mode=4 hdmi_force_hotplug=1 hdmi_drive=2` is the known-good reference.
- Pixel rate: 74.25 MHz (standard CEA-861 VIC 4 / 720p60).

Full-range vs limited-range is sender-controlled. TC358743's AVI InfoFrame carries whatever the source advertises; currently Pi sends limited-range, so peak values in DDR are `0xFE` not `0xFF`. EDID colorimetry overrides are a separate future task.

### 2.2 TC358743 HDMI-to-CSI-2 bridge

Driver: `firmware/marvin/default/src/tc358743.c`. Register values derived from mainline Linux `tc358743.c`.

| Register | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `PLLCTL` PRD=4, FBD=144 | PLL out = 972 MHz | `hsck = (27 MHz / PRD) × FBD` |
| `CSI_CONFW` lanes | 2 | 2 data lanes × 972 Mbps = 1.944 Gbps total (plenty for 720p60 RGB888's ~1.33 Gbps) |
| `CONFCTL` | 0x0007 | PCLK divider off, 3-byte pixel pack, no audio |
| `FIFOCTL` | 0x0176 | FIFO level 374 (kernel hardcodes at all rates) |
| `VI_MODE` | 0xE6 | RGB888 input, 16-bit HDMI RX side |
| `VI_REP`  | 0x00 | **No pixel replication / doubling** (critical — was 0x80 in earlier 480p test and caused 16-row phase drift) |
| `VOUT_SET2` / `VOUT_SET3` | 0x01 / 0x08 | Output color format / range handling |
| CSI-2 DT | 0x24 | RGB888 per CSI-2 spec |

D-PHY timing (for 972 Mbps):
\```
LINEINITCNT  = 0x1B58
LPTXTIMECNT  = 0x0007
TCLK_HEADER  = 0x2806    TCLK_TRAIL  = 0x0000    TCLK_POST = 0x0008
THS_HEADER   = 0x0806    THS_TRAIL   = 0x0005
TWAKEUP      = 0x4268    HSTXVREGCNT = 0x0000
\```

Operating mode: **continuous clock** (`TXOPTIONCNTRL = CONTCLKMODE`). This is the required-match with the SAM9X75 RX side — if RX expects gated but TX sends continuous (or vice versa), `CSI2DC.GSR.ARSTIP` hangs permanently.

### 2.3 SAM9X75 MIPI CSI-2 D-PHY RX

Driver: `firmware/marvin/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/csi/` (MCC-generated, slightly tweaked).

Key setting — **the one parameter that took us the longest to get right**:

\```c
// isc_capture.c:25
#define ISC_CAP_CSI_BITRATE  0x0Au
\```

This is the `HSFREQRANGE` DWC D-PHY test-mode value. SAM9X75 is **DWC Gen3** (verified from Linux DT: `snps,dw-dphy-rx` with `snps,phy_type=<0>`). The Gen3 table entry for the 950–1000 Mbps band is `0x0A`.

- **Wrong** (used during earlier debug): `0x1A` — that's a Gen2 value. At 972 Mbps Gen2 bands diverge from Gen3, symptom is persistent `PHY_FATAL.SOT_SYNC_ERR = 0x3`.
- **Correct** for 972 Mbps Gen3: `0x0A`.
- Changes with bitrate. If bitrate moves, look up Gen3 table (DesignWare MIPI D-PHY RX Gen3 Databook), don't copy values from other SoC examples.

Other CSI settings:
- `CSI_NUM_LANES = 2` (matches TC358743).
- `csiObj->csiFps = 60u` (informational; drives some timing in the driver).

### 2.4 CSI2DC — the RMS=0 lever

**This is the key decision that enables in-pipeline BGRX32.** DS60001813 §49.6.54:

| VPCFGR Field | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| DT (bits 5:0) | 0x24 | RGB888 (matches TC358743 emission) |
| VC (bits 7:6) | 0 | Virtual channel 0 |
| PA (bit 14) | **0** | LSB-aligned. PA=1 is for 10/12-bit Bayer sensors being packed onto ISC's 12-bit internal bus. Irrelevant for MIPI RGB888 bypass. |
| **RMS (bit 13)** | **0** | **Critical.** See below. |
| RGB36MAP (bit 15) | 0 | Use Table 49.25 pixel mapping |

`RMS` (Recommended Memory Storage) per datasheet:

- `RMS=0` — "CSI2DC outputs 1 pixel per component per clock cycle, compliant with the ISC processing engine." → Table 49.25: `demux_data[39:24]=0`, `[23:16]=R`, `[15:8]=G`, `[7:0]=B`. **One pixel per 40-bit VP word.**
- `RMS=1` — "CSI2DC generates a byte stream compliant with the CSI-2 specification memory format." → Table 49.27: 4 BGR pixels packed into 12 bytes. This is what MCC's default config produces — results in **dense 3 B/pixel BGR** (not what we want for direct display).

**MCC hardcodes RMS=1.** We override it:

\```c
// firmware/marvin/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/csi2dc/plib_csi2dc.c
void CSI2DC_Configure_VideoPipe(uint32_t dt, uint32_t vc, uint32_t align_isc) {
    CSI2DC_REGS->CSI2DC_VPCFGR = CSI2DC_VPCFGR_DT(dt)
                               | CSI2DC_VPCFGR_VC(vc)
                               | (align_isc ? CSI2DC_VPCFGR_PA_1 : 0);
    /* NOTE: do NOT OR in CSI2DC_VPCFGR_RMS_1 — we want RMS=0 so each pixel
     *       occupies a full 40-bit VP word with the low 32 bits = 0x00RRGGBB. */
}
\```

Other CSI2DC config:
- `GCFGR.MIPIFRN = 0` (free-running, matches TC358743's continuous-clock mode). MCC default is gated (`MIPIFRN=1`); mismatch leaves `CSI2DC.GSR.ARSTIP` stuck on reset. Override via `csi2dcObj->enableMIPIFreeRun = true;` in `isc_capture.c:91`.
- `VPER = 1` (video pipe enabled).

### 2.5 ISC — Parallel Front End (PFE)

DS60001813 §50.6.6, §50.7.4–50.7.6.

Key settings configured by `DRV_ISC_Configure()`:

| PFE_CFG0 field | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| REP | 0 | N/A for BPS=FORTY |
| BPS (30:28) | 5 = FORTY | "40-bit input (used for MIPI formats up to forty bits per pixel)." Matches CSI2DC's 40-bit VP bus. |
| MIPI (bit 14) | 1 | Input from MIPI interface |
| GATED (bit 8) | 0 | Free-running clock |
| CCIR656 (bit 9) | 0 | Not embedded-sync — using MIPI |
| CONT (bit 7) | 1 | Continuous acquisition (vs single shot) |
| MODE (6:4) | 0 = PROGRESSIVE | Source is progressive |
| VPOL / HPOL | 0 | Active-high sync (standard) |

**Two bits that MCC leaves OFF but we must set:**

| PFE_CFG0 field | Value | Why MCC misses it |
|---|---|---|
| **COLEN (bit 12)** | **1** | Enables the column crop window |
| **ROWEN (bit 13)** | **1** | Enables the row crop window |

MCC's `ISC_PFE_Crop_Area()` function is defined in `plib_isc.c` but **never called**. Without COLEN+ROWEN and valid COLMAX/ROWMAX, the PFE expects a 1×1 frame and fires HDTO (Horizontal Detection Timeout) on the first real line. The Linux `mchp-isc` driver sets both bits; we match that.

We program these directly after `DRV_ISC_Configure()`:

\```c
// isc_capture.c:204-209
ISC_REGS->ISC_PFE_CFG1 = ISC_PFE_CFG1_COLMIN(0u)
                       | ISC_PFE_CFG1_COLMAX((uint32_t)width - 1u);   // 1279 at 720p
ISC_REGS->ISC_PFE_CFG2 = ISC_PFE_CFG2_ROWMIN(0u)
                       | ISC_PFE_CFG2_ROWMAX((uint32_t)height - 1u);  // 719  at 720p
ISC_REGS->ISC_PFE_CFG0 |= ISC_PFE_CFG0_COLEN_1 | ISC_PFE_CFG0_ROWEN_1;
\```

With RMS=0, COLMAX is in **pixel units** (1 sample per pixel). Under the previous RMS=1 path, COLMAX was `(W × 3) / 4 - 1` because the ISC counted 32-bit byte-stream words.

### 2.6 ISC — Rounding, Limiting, Packing (RLP)

DS60001813 §50.6.19, §50.7.67.

| RLP_CFG field | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **MODE (3:0)** | **15 = BYPASS** | "32-bit input is sampled and written to the rlp output port. Select this mode for MIPI RMS mode." Passes `sub420_data[31:0]` through unchanged. With our RMS=0 input that's `0x00RRGGBB`. |
| ALPHA (15:8) | — | Ignored in BYPASS mode (only used by ARGB444/ARGB555/ARGB32 modes) |
| YMODE / LSH / REP | 0 | Not applicable to BYPASS |

**Why not ARGB32 RLP (Mode 10)?** Per §50.6.19 Table row for RGB32/ARGB32:
\```
rlp_data[31:24] = A = ALPHA[7:0]       (register)
rlp_data[23:16] = R = sub420_data[29:22]
rlp_data[15:8]  = G = sub420_data[19:12]
rlp_data[7:0]   = B = sub420_data[9:2]
\```

These bit positions are the output format of the ISC **CSC module** (Color Space Conversion, §50.6.15), not raw MIPI RGB888. On our bypass path, R/G/B sit at `[23:16]/[15:8]/[7:0]` — a 6/4/2-bit shift off what ARGB32 RLP wants. Attempting it yields mangled 3-shifted-copies-of-garbage per 12 bytes. **ARGB32 RLP is structurally unusable for MIPI RGB888 bypass;** it would require enabling the full demosaic pipeline (for Bayer sources) or CSC (for YCbCr).

Consequence: we cannot get `alpha = 0xFF` in-pipeline for free. We get `alpha = 0x00` because CSI2DC zeros the upper 16 bits of each 40-bit VP word. If `0xFF` alpha matters, a one-shot CPU pass to set `buf[3::4] = 0xFF` does it cheaply, or stamp 0xFF into the framebuffer once at init (DMA writes never touch byte 3 if pixel stride matches — need to verify that assumption before relying on it).

**Driver hint:** `iscObj->rlpMode = ISC_RLP_CFG_MODE_BYPASS` (value 15 in the MCC enum). `drv_isc.c` writes this into RLP_CFG during `DRV_ISC_Configure`.

### 2.7 ISC — DMA Host

DS60001813 §50.6.20, §50.7.70.

| DCFG field | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **IMODE (2:0)** | **2 = PACKED32** | "32 bits, single channel packed." Stores each `rlp_data[31:0]` as 4 contiguous bytes in memory. Little-endian → `B G R 00`. |
| YMBSIZE (6:4) | 4 = BEATS32 | 32-beat AXI burst (sama7g5 / SAM9X7 — MCC's PACKED8 default is BEATS8 which is the sama5d2 value, undersized for this SoC). |
| CMBSIZE (10:8) | 4 = BEATS32 | Same rationale as YMBSIZE. |
| ARQOS / AWQOS | 0 | Dynamic QoS based on FIFO level (recommended default) |

MCC's `DRV_ISC_Configure` sets PACKED8 + BEATS8 if `iscObj->layout = ISC_LAYOUT_PACKED8`. We override after `DRV_ISC_Configure`:

\```c
// isc_capture.c:219-221
ISC_REGS->ISC_DCFG = ISC_DCFG_IMODE_PACKED32
                   | ISC_DCFG_YMBSIZE_BEATS32
                   | ISC_DCFG_CMBSIZE_BEATS32;
\```

The write is safe because nothing in MCC writes DCFG again after this point (the redundant-call to `DRV_ISC_Configure_DMA` was removed). `DRV_ISC_Configure` already calls it internally at `drv_isc.c:381` — don't add a second call.

**Descriptor view:** `DCTRL.DVIEW = 0` (PACKED / single channel). `DAD0` holds the current buffer base address. `DST0` = 0 (contiguous frame, no row stride gap).

### 2.8 Framebuffer layout in DDR

\```c
// isc_capture.c:17-29
#define ISC_CAP_MAX_W        1920u
#define ISC_CAP_MAX_H        1080u
#define ISC_CAP_BPP          4u      /* BGRX32 */
#define ISC_CAP_NUM_BUFFERS  2u

static __attribute__((__section__(".region_cache_aligned")))
       __attribute__((__aligned__(32)))
       uint8_t g_framebuffer[ISC_CAP_MAX_W * ISC_CAP_MAX_H * ISC_CAP_BPP * ISC_CAP_NUM_BUFFERS];
\```

- Pool size: 1920×1080×4×2 = 16.6 MB, in the cacheable DDR region.
- 32-byte aligned (cache line boundary for ARM926 L1).
- At 720p: only 3,686,400 B × 2 = 7.37 MB actually used.
- Double-buffered for tear-free consumption by the display stage (ISR toggles `frameIndex`; probe reads the *previous* completed buffer).

Pixel access pattern (0-indexed, little-endian):

\```c
uint8_t *px = &g_framebuffer[(y * W + x) * 4];
uint8_t B = px[0];
uint8_t G = px[1];
uint8_t R = px[2];
// px[3] = 0x00 (X / unused)
\```

As a 32-bit word: `*(uint32_t*)px == 0x00RRGGBB` (native little-endian).

---

## 3. Verified output — color sweep

Pi source, 720p60 RGB limited-range (so peak = 0xFE). Probe reports memory at representative points across the frame:

| Source color | Memory (`b0 b1 b2 b3`) | Decode |
|---|---|---|
| Red   | `00 00 FE 00` | B=0, G=0, R=0xFE, X=0 |
| Green | `00 FE 00 00` | B=0, G=0xFE, R=0, X=0 |
| Blue  | `FE 00 00 00` | B=0xFE, G=0, R=0, X=0 |
| White | `FE FE FE 00` | B=G=R=0xFE, X=0 |
| Black | `00 00 00 00` | — |

All five match expectation across the full 1280×720 extent (rows 0..719 completely written, no cliff). Framerate sustained at 70 fps probe-window average (≈60 fps real + diagnostic ticks).

---

## 4. Where each override lives in code

| Stage | File | Line | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| TC358743 D-PHY timing | `default/src/tc358743.c` | 25–33 | 972 Mbps timing constants (kernel-derived) |
| TC358743 PLL | `default/src/tc358743.c` | 14–20 | `PLL_PRD=4`, `PLL_FBD=144` |
| CSI HSFREQRANGE | `default/src/isc_capture.c` | 25 | `0x0A` for DWC Gen3 @ 972 Mbps |
| CSI bitrate override | `default/src/isc_capture.c` | 86 | `csiObj->csiBitRate = ISC_CAP_CSI_BITRATE` (MCC default is `0x16`) |
| CSI2DC RMS=0 | `default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/csi2dc/plib_csi2dc.c` | 71–78 | dropped `CSI2DC_VPCFGR_RMS_1` from VPCFGR write |
| CSI2DC free-run | `default/src/isc_capture.c` | 91 | `enableMIPIFreeRun = true` |
| ISC PFE crop | `default/src/isc_capture.c` | 204–209 | direct `PFE_CFG1/2` + `COLEN`/`ROWEN` writes |
| ISC DMA config | `default/src/isc_capture.c` | 219–221 | direct `DCFG` write (PACKED32 + BEATS32×2) |
| Framebuffer BPP | `default/src/isc_capture.c` | 19 | `ISC_CAP_BPP = 4` |

---

## 5. Debug / diagnostics

`ISC_Capture_ProbeFrame()` in `isc_capture.c` dumps once per second:

1. **`cliff:` block** — PFE/DMA register snapshot, INTSR decode with named bits (VD/HD/DDONE/LDONE/HDTO/VDTO/DAOV/BUSERR), per-probe frame-counter deltas.
2. **`IDS[i]:`** — CSI2DC Image Data Snoop per-packet metadata: DT / VC / word-count (bytes per MIPI long packet) / accumulated row count since last snoop reset. Authoritative per-packet evidence of what CSI-2 sent us. `WC=3840` at 720p = 1280 px × 3 MIPI bytes/pixel = correct.
3. **9-point mem dump** — 4-byte samples at `{TL,TM,TR,ML,CT,MR,BL,BM,BR}` of the frame. First diagnostic to check when reasoning about pixel format.
4. **Hex rows** — 48 bytes × 5 row locations for visual inspection of packing.
5. **Byte-range scan** — min/max of each byte position across row 30. Useful for detecting whether data is present at all.
6. **Vertical extent** — first unwritten row (sentinel 0x55 = DMA never touched). Full frame expected = `rows 0..719 written, first sentinel at row 720 (of 720)`.
7. **Phase scan** — reports the mod-BPP byte-lane offset of the first saturated byte per row. Useful legacy diagnostic from the RMS=1 phase-drift days; with BGRX32 it's pretty much constant per solid color.

When something's wrong, read in this order:
- `INTSR` error bits (HDTO/VDTO/DAOV/BUSERR) point at the PFE, PFE, DMA, or bus respectively.
- `IDS[0]` WC and rows tell you if CSI-2 payload is correct at the wire level.
- 9-point dump + row-30 range localize format/byte-order issues.
- `vertical extent` distinguishes a cliff from a format issue.

---

## 6. Known carry-forwards

- **`INTSR.HDTO` always set** after capture start — informational-only residual, not a stop signal. Also present under working RMS=1 config. Safe to ignore.
- **`frameIndex` stuck at 0** in most probe windows — DDONE interrupt fires rarely or not at all, but the DMA itself works (buffers update, `frameCount` counts VDs at correct rate). Investigate before relying on DDONE-based downstream triggers.
- **Pixel range 0x00–0xFE** because TC358743 passes through source's limited-range signaling. EDID overrides or TC358743 colorimetry registers can force full-range; deferred until display stage forces the issue.
- **Alpha channel = 0x00** — not 0xFF. Acceptable for display framebuffers that ignore alpha; requires CPU fix-up if alpha is semantic.

---

## 7. Datasheet-anchored reasoning for ARGB/RGBA aspirations

If someone revisits this and asks "can we get ARGB32 directly in-pipeline?":

1. **ARGB32 RLP mode** requires upstream data at `sub420_data[29:22]/[19:12]/[9:2]`. That's the CSC output format (§50.6.15). CSC is a module for converting to/from YCbCr — it's not a pass-through. Routing RGB888 through CSC would work only if CSC has an identity-RGB mode, which per §50.6.15 it doesn't (the CSC input is YCbCr by design).
2. **Demosaic pipeline** (WB → CFA → CC → GAM → …) expects 10/12-bit Bayer mosaic input, not 24-bit RGB.
3. **CSI2DC has no alpha-insertion register** — only RMS mode and the RGB36MAP packing variant. Neither affects the upper byte.

Therefore the cleanest path to ARGB32 is:
- **Software post-pass:** single `memset` of byte 3 at framebuffer init (if DMA stride matches) or a per-frame byte-smearing pass (expensive).
- **GFX2D blit:** use the 2D graphics engine to copy BGRX32 → ARGB32 with alpha fill. Zero CPU cost if the engine supports it.
- **Display IP native BGRX support:** SAM9X75 LCDC supports multiple BGRX/ARGB layouts — pick one that doesn't care about alpha. Probably the right answer.

```

Let me think through this carefully before proposing.

## What actually fixed the pipeline?

Today's `RMS=0 + PACKED32 + COLMAX=W-1` change was a **packing reshape** (dense 3 B/pixel BGR → BGRX32 4 B/pixel). The data content was already correct going in.

The *real* breakthrough that made RGB888 data land in memory intact was earlier — commit `2908679` (**BPS=FORTY**). Before that, the ISC was treating the 40-bit CSI2DC word as 8-bit bytes and slicing pixels at bit boundaries (the "bit-spread 12-byte-per-pixel" garbage). After BPS=FORTY, ISC correctly accepted the 40-bit-wide MIPI word; from that moment on data in DDR was recoverable.

So the ordered list of decisive changes — with 480p lens:

| Fix | Resolution-agnostic? | Applies to 480p? |
|---|---|---|
| `HSFREQRANGE = 0x0A` (DWC Gen3 for 972 Mbps) | No — bitrate-specific | 480p uses 297 Mbps → different HSFREQRANGE value |
| `PFE_CFG1/2` crop + `COLEN/ROWEN` | ✅ Yes | Yes — journal line 611 literally says "almost certainly been happening on 480p too" |
| `DCFG = PACKED32 + BEATS32` | ✅ Yes | Yes |
| **`BPS = FORTY`** (the big one) | ✅ Yes | Yes — never tested at 480p |
| `RMS = 0` (today) | ✅ Yes | Yes |

## The 480p question: what likely happens now?

Per journal line 640, 720p's phase drift vanished at 972 Mbps. The 480p drift was attributed to *"pixel-doubling path, or the 297 Mbps/lane CSI rate, or both"* — but **480p was never re-tested with BPS=FORTY**. At the time, the capture pipeline was still misconfigured (BPS=EIGHT + RMS=1 byte-stream + no PFE crop + wrong burst size). It's plausible that some fraction of what looked like "phase drift" was actually BPS=EIGHT misinterpreting 40-bit word boundaries on a different pixel cadence — I can't prove it without a bench test, but I also can't rule it out.

What's definitely true: today's capture config is resolution-agnostic. Changing `width`/`height` in `ISC_Capture_Configure` is enough on the ISC side — PFE crop, DMA size, and framebuffer offsets all scale.

## Plan for 480p revisit

Three variables to isolate, in order of cheapness:

**Phase A — current 720p, just baseline** (sanity — confirm nothing regressed).

**Phase B — Pi @ 480p, 972 Mbps retained.** Simplest: change Pi config.txt to `hdmi_mode=1` (640×480) or `hdmi_mode=2` (720×480), re-add 480p to the TC358743 EDID, reduce `ISC_Capture_Configure` width/height. Keep CSI rate at 972 Mbps (TC358743 will pad blanking to sustain it — the kernel driver does this; journal line 460 already notes we'll inherit that approach).
- If drift is gone → it was either pixel-doubling (from Wii specifically) or 297 Mbps PHY alignment. Either way we have clean 480p.
- If drift persists → it's something intrinsic to the 480p packet stream (line count, HBlank, etc.) and we look at CSI2DC GCFGR.ULC / Data Pipe path (journal line 712 noted these were never tested).

**Phase C — Wii @ 480p through ElectronWarp.** The original use case. Only after Phase B confirms 480p itself is clean, so we know any remaining drift is specifically the component-to-HDMI conversion chain, not resolution.

**Work items:**

1. **TC358743 D-PHY timing at 480p** — three options, pick after Phase A:
   - Keep 972 Mbps (simplest; let TC358743 pad). Zero changes in `tc358743.c`.
   - Drop to 297 Mbps (original 480p config). Requires PLL_FBD change and new D-PHY timing constants (kernel driver has the 297 Mbps table). `ISC_CAP_CSI_BITRATE` changes from `0x0A` back to the appropriate Gen3 value for ~250–300 Mbps band.
   - Match kernel's 594 Mbps minimum for 480p.
2. **EDID** — add 480p DTD/VIC back in (CEA VDB VIC 1/2/3). Currently 720p-only to force source off 480p.
3. **Pi config.txt** for 480p — documented known-good setting.
4. **Framebuffer size sanity** — at 480p we're using a fraction of the `MAX_W × MAX_H × 4 × 2` pool, fine.
5. **Probe phase-scanner interpretation update** — today's probe uses `b % ISC_CAP_BPP` which is right for BGRX32; historical 480p drift was seen with 3 B/pixel RMS=1 mode, so cross-resolution comparison needs that caveat noted.

441	#### Phase 6 — First rendered frame
442	
443	Goal: pixels in SDRAM (Phase 5 output) shown on the Legato LCD surface already brought up in commit `3bb441a`.
444	
445	**Scope / known items to work through:**
446	
447	- **Cache coherence.** Framebuffer is `.region_cache_aligned` (cached DDR). DMA writes bypass CPU cache, so CPU-side reads will see stale data unless we invalidate the cache range before reading each frame. Use `SYS_CACHE_InvalidateDCache_by_Addr(addr, size)` keyed off the frame-done callback. Alternative: move framebuffer to `.region_nocache` — simpler but trades off uncached-read latency.
448	- **Double-buffered swap.** ISC DMA writes alternately to buffer 0 and buffer 1 (`dmaDescSize=2`, `frameIndex` wraps in `ISC_Handler`). Renderer should read the *previously completed* buffer (`(frameIndex + 1) & 1` from the callback's perspective) so it doesn't race the in-flight DMA write.
449	- **Limited-range → full-range RGB.** Wii outputs 16-235 (SMPTE limited). Legato renders 0-255 full range. Without expansion, blacks look gray and whites dim. Simple linear expand: `out = ((in - 16) * 255) / 219`, clamped. Decide whether to do this in a fast SIMD loop on ARM9 or use the 2D GPU (commit `5cd5a90` brought that in) for a blit-time conversion.
450	- **Legato integration.** Probably an `Image Widget` pointed at our framebuffer, set to paint on each `le_RedrawAll()`. Or a custom widget if we need per-pixel control. Need to check Legato's pixel-format support — ARGB32 is standard, but its buffer descriptor conventions are worth looking up.
451	- **Redraw cadence vs. capture cadence.** ISC is pushing frames at 60 Hz. LCD refresh is likely also 60 Hz (Legato default, depends on `drv_gfx_xlcdc` config). Want to request a redraw *on* each new-frame callback rather than polling Legato's own tick. Avoid double-buffer tears.
452	- **Display resolution vs. source resolution.** Wii is 720×480. LCD module `AC69T88A` (from commit `3bb441a`) is 1024×600 per the emirror reference. Options: center + letterbox (simplest), stretch-to-fit (use 2D GPU scaler), or 1:1 pixel map with blanks. Start with letterbox for sanity, revisit if we want fullscreen.
453	- **Frame counter / metrics on screen.** Optional: overlay `ISC: N fps` on the display for at-a-glance debugging without needing DBGU.
454	- **Source mode robustness.** If the Wii resets and outputs a different mode (e.g. 1440×240p from an earlier observation), the capture pipeline re-configures automatically, but the renderer needs to handle a resolution change mid-run. Either re-create the image widget on `TC358743_GetDetectedFormat` change, or make the renderer resolution-aware.
455	
456	None of this blocks anything — it's just things to think about before wiring up the render path.
457	
458	### Known risks
459	
460	1. **TC358743 CSI-TX minimum bitrate.** At 480p60 the native pixel rate is low enough that the Linux driver runs CSI-TX faster than the source and pads with blanking. We'll likely inherit that approach, and SAM9X75 ISC must tolerate it.
461	2. **ISC ↔ TC358743 handshake.** ISC expects specific CSI-2 frame-start/frame-end conventions. Format tag mismatches (YUV422 8-bit vs 10-bit, etc.) manifest as "no frames" and are painful to debug.
462	3. **EDID.** If the Wii sees a bad/missing EDID it may fall back to 480i or refuse to output. Test the source independently before blaming the driver.
463	
464	---
465	
466	## Decision log
467	
468	| Date | Decision | Rationale |
469	|------|----------|-----------|
470	| 2026-05-01 | First real driver work is the TC358743 HDMI-to-CSI bridge | It's the gate between hardware-wired and pixels-in-memory. Everything downstream (vision, actuation) depends on it. |
471	| 2026-05-01 | Reference source = mainline Linux tc358743 driver + community 480p dumps | Linux driver has correct state machine / EDID / IRQ handling; community dumps have verified 480p register values. |
472	| 2026-05-01 | Integration shape (sensor vs standalone) deferred until Phase 3 | Avoid premature structure; real answer depends on how much state the driver actually needs. |
473	| 2026-05-01 | Journal lives at `firmware/marvin/docs/journal.md` | Firmware docs co-located with firmware; top-level `docs/` is hardware/mechanical. |
474	| 2026-05-01 | TC358743 I2C address: **`0x0f`** (7-bit) | Matches the in-tree kernel DT example (`imx6q-h100.dts:190`, `tc358743@f`) and the Waveshare v1/v2 default tie-off. Confirm by I2C bus scan during Phase 1 bring-up. |
475	| 2026-05-01 | REFCLK: **27 MHz** | Waveshare v1/v2 on-board XTAL. Kernel driver restricts REFCLK to {26, 27, 42} MHz (`tc358743.c:717-719`); 27 MHz is the Waveshare v1/v2 value. |
476	| 2026-05-01 | Target CSI-2 output format: **RGB888** (MIPI data type `0x24`) | Marvin pipeline is already configured for RGB888 end-to-end: `CSI_DATA_FORMAT_TYPE = CSI2_DATA_FORMAT_RGB888`, ISC input RGB 8-bit, CSI2DC pipes RGB888, ISC output ARGB32. Emitting YUV from TC358743 would require reconfiguring ISC/CSI2DC — staying with RGB is cheaper. |
477	| 2026-05-01 | Register-access helpers will be a direct port from the kernel driver | `tc358743.c:131-269` has clean `i2c_rd/wr` + `i2c_rd8/wr8/rd16/wr16/rd32/wr32`. Map to FLEXCOM6 TWI underneath. |
478	| 2026-05-01 | J29 (22-pin MIPI) pinout confirmed; PC19=pin 17, PC15=pin 18 (not 5/6) | Per SAM9X75-Curiosity User Guide §3.4.10 (queried via Microchip MCP). Pins 5/6 are MIPI_D1_N/P — CSI data lane 1 diff pairs, not GPIOs. Correct GPIO pins for RESET/INT are pin 17 (PC19, `MIPI_CSI_GPIO0`) and pin 18 (PC15, `MIPI_CSI_GPIO1`). I2C on pins 20 (PA25, `CAM_I²C_CLK`) and 21 (PA24, `CAM_I²C_DATA`) confirmed to match marvin's FLEXCOM6 pin assignment (`pin_configurations.csv:85-86`). |
479	| 2026-05-01 | Phase 1 will drive RESET via software (I2C `SYSCTL.Sreset`), not via GPIO | Even if PC19 reaches the 15-pin side through the adapter, Waveshare v1/v2 typically does NOT route TC358743 `RESET_N` out to the 15-pin FFC — the chip's reset is an on-board RC/POR network. Software reset over I2C is always available and is what the kernel driver uses. Means we don't need to validate the GPIO path before Phase 1 bring-up. |
480	| 2026-05-01 | Delays use Harmony's `SYS_TIME` service (non-blocking shape) | Already initialized in `SYS_Initialize`; existing marvin code (`drv_isc.c`, `plib_isc.c`) uses it with `SYS_TIME_DelayUS/MS` + `SYS_TIME_DelayIsComplete`. Non-blocking pattern inside our state machine keeps `APP_Tasks()` (and Legato) from stalling during reset hold times, and scales naturally into Phase 3's longer init sequence. |
481	| 2026-05-01 | Our I2C open uses `DRV_IO_INTENT_READWRITE`, not `EXCLUSIVE` | `EXCLUSIVE` is rejected by Harmony's I2C driver if any other client is already open. Even after libcamera is removed we prefer `READWRITE` so our module can coexist with any future MCC-generated I2C client. `DRV_I2C_CLIENTS_NUMBER_IDX0 = 2` in `configuration.h` already permits multi-client use. |
482	| 2026-05-01 | Libcamera (Camera Module + Image Sensor Driver + Vision Camera Library) to be removed from MCC | Conflicts with TC358743 bridge approach: libcamera expects a directly-attached sensor (IMX219/OV5640/etc.), probes them at boot (adds bus traffic + console noise), and configures ISC/CSI/CSI2DC with sensor-style assumptions that we'll need to override in Phase 3. Keeping CSI/ISC/CSI2DC peripheral/driver layers — we'll drive those directly from the TC358743 module. Greg regenerating MCC. |
483	| 2026-05-01 | Post-regen: keep a minimal `drv_image_sensor.h` shim at the original path | ISC driver (`drv_isc.c:15, 246, 257, 363-365`) and `configuration.h:106-107` reference `DRV_IMAGE_SENSOR_*` enum values that MCC didn't scrub when the image-sensor component was removed. Shim defines just the enum values used (exact numeric equivalence to originals). Lives at the MCC-generated path because `drv_isc.c`'s include is hardcoded — but MCC no longer regenerates that directory, so the shim is stable. |

Define it as a compile flag instead of editing `configuration.h` (MCC-regenerated) — `user.cmake` survives regens. Value `0` elides the debug prints entirely; if we ever need them, bump to `1`. |

Rather than modifying MCC-generated code, we treat the MCC value as a default and override in `isc_capture` alongside the already-necessary `csiFrameWidth/Height/Fps` overrides. Only one MCC-file modification stays (`plib_csi.c` `CSI_Analog_Init` bug fix). |

_**User (2026-05-02 21:41:15Z)**_

how do I modify rpi configuration for 720x480@60?

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 21:41:24Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 21:41:31Z)**_

On the Pi's SD card, edit `/boot/firmware/config.txt` (older Pi OS: `/boot/config.txt`). Change to:

```
hdmi_force_hotplug=1
hdmi_group=1
hdmi_mode=2
hdmi_drive=2
```

- `hdmi_group=1` → CEA modes
- `hdmi_mode=2` → **720×480p @ 60 Hz, 4:3** (CEA VIC 2)
- Use `hdmi_mode=3` instead if you want 16:9 (VIC 3); `hdmi_mode=1` for 640×480p60 (VIC 1).
- `hdmi_force_hotplug=1` keeps output alive if the bridge isn't asserting HPD yet.
- `hdmi_drive=2` = HDMI (vs DVI) signaling.

If you also want to kill the KMS driver's negotiation (we did this for 720p to stop it re-picking a mode), comment out `dtoverlay=vc4-kms-v3d` (or `vc4-fkms-v3d`) in the same file.

Reboot the Pi after editing. On next boot, verify from the Pi shell with:
```
tvservice -s        # shows active mode
vcgencmd hdmi_timings
```

Then power-cycle the TC358743 chain and watch the marvin DBGU for `TC358743: detected 720x480p @ 60 Hz`. Note: our current EDID only advertises 720p60 (VIC 4/19/34) — the Pi will see no 480p support and will probably **ignore** `hdmi_mode=2` and fall back to 720p. For Phase 7a we need to re-add a 480p DTD + CEA VIC to the TC358743 EDID first, otherwise this config.txt change won't take effect.

is hdmi_mode correct? you say 720x480 is 4:3 and 640x480 is 16:9?

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 21:58:52Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 21:58:56Z)**_

Re-reading my message — I said `hdmi_mode=2` is 720×480 4:3, `hdmi_mode=3` is 720×480 16:9, and `hdmi_mode=1` is 640×480 (I didn't label its aspect). I didn't say 640×480 was 16:9.

For clarity, the CEA-861 VICs the Pi's `hdmi_group=1` maps to are:

| `hdmi_mode` | VIC | Resolution | Aspect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 640×480p60 | **4:3** |
| 2 | 2 | 720×480p60 | **4:3** |
| 3 | 3 | 720×480p60 | **16:9** |
| 4 | 4 | 1280×720p60 | 16:9 |

So VIC 2 and VIC 3 are the *same* 720×480 pixels — only the advertised aspect ratio differs (the AVI InfoFrame tells the sink how to letterbox/scale). For capture into a 720×480 buffer, aspect ratio is cosmetic; pick whichever matches the content.

For our Wii path historically we used VIC 2 (4:3, matches the console's native 4:3 content).

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 22:02:47Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 22:02:53Z)**_

Right — `tvservice` was deprecated when Pi OS switched to KMS (bookworm+). Use one of these instead:

```bash
# Active mode + connector status (KMS/DRM world):
kmsprint                    # from libdrm-tests; apt install libdrm-tests if missing

# Or via the DRM sysfs:
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-*/modes | head -5
cat /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-*/status

# modetest is the most detailed (shows current mode + all supported modes):
modetest -M vc4 -c          # apt install libdrm-tests
```

If you're still getting `tvservice not found`, you're on KMS. If you want the old `tvservice`-style behavior back (simpler for debug), either switch to the legacy driver by setting `dtoverlay=vc4-fkms-v3d` → comment it out, OR add `dtoverlay=vc4-fkms-v3d,composite=1` depending on Pi model. But really — `modetest -M vc4 -c` gives more info than `tvservice` ever did.

Quick one-liner for "what's the Pi actually outputting right now":
```bash
modetest -M vc4 -c 2>/dev/null | awk '/HDMI-A/,/connectors/' | grep -A2 "^  [0-9]"
```

_**User (2026-05-02 22:04:45Z)**_

failed to open device vc4

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 22:04:49Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 22:04:52Z)**_

Try in this order:

```bash
# 1. Needs root for /dev/dri access on most setups:
sudo modetest -M vc4 -c

# 2. If "no such device" — the driver module name differs (Pi 5 uses v3d/vc4 split, older Pis sometimes need different name):
ls /sys/class/drm/                 # shows cards present
sudo modetest -c                   # without -M, auto-probes all DRM devices

# 3. Fallback — no modetest at all, read DRM sysfs directly:
for c in /sys/class/drm/card*-HDMI-A-*/; do
  echo "=== $c ==="
  cat "$c/status"
  head -5 "$c/modes"
done
```

The sysfs approach (#3) works with zero extra packages and tells you the active connector + top modes offered by the sink's EDID. First line of `modes` is typically the preferred/current mode.

But honestly — the authoritative check is the marvin DBGU line:

```
TC358743: detected 720x480p @ 60 Hz, ...

That's what actually matters. Edit config.txt, reboot the Pi, watch marvin's serial output on the next HPD cycle. If it reports 720x480p — it's working regardless of what the Pi itself says about its output.

Reminder: our current EDID only advertises 720p60 (VIC 4/19/34). Until you add a 480p DTD+VIC back to the TC358743 EDID, the Pi will see no 480p offer in the EDID and will almost certainly stay at 720p. So the `hdmi_mode=2` alone won't do it — the EDID change is the actual gate.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 22:08:30Z)**_

Yep — same BGRX trick through `/dev/fb0`. For 720×480:

```bash
sudo python3 -c "open('/dev/fb0','wb').write(b'\x00\x00\xff\x00' * (720*480))"
```

Byte order = `B G R X` = `00 00 FF 00` → full red.

For the other primaries:

```bash
# Green:
sudo python3 -c "open('/dev/fb0','wb').write(b'\x00\xff\x00\x00' * (720*480))"

# Blue:
sudo python3 -c "open('/dev/fb0','wb').write(b'\xff\x00\x00\x00' * (720*480))"

# White:
sudo python3 -c "open('/dev/fb0','wb').write(b'\xff\xff\xff\x00' * (720*480))"

# Black:
sudo python3 -c "open('/dev/fb0','wb').write(b'\x00\x00\x00\x00' * (720*480))"
```

If the console cursor / login prompt keeps overwriting, hide the cursor first:

```bash
sudo sh -c 'echo 0 > /sys/class/graphics/fbcon/cursor_blink'    # if available
# or switch to unused tty:
sudo chvt 3
```

If `/dev/fb0` is a different size than 720×480 (the Pi's framebuffer might be set to something else depending on overscan / config), check first:

```bash
fbset -i | grep geometry       # shows actual fb size
```

and scale the pixel count accordingly.

**That's huge.** 480p works cleanly on the first try. No firmware changes required — capture auto-reconfigured from the TC358743-detected format.

Verification:
- `raster 858x525` — correct standard NTSC 480p raster
- `WC=2160 rows=480` — 720 px × 3 MIPI bytes × 480 rows, full frame
- `1,382,400 B/frame` = 720 × 480 × 4 ✓

- `vertical extent: rows 0..479 written`
- **Phase scanner: one entry only (`row 0 → 2`). The 5/11 16-row drift is gone.**

**The historical 480p drift was not intrinsic to 480p resolution.** It was the broken pipeline — BPS=EIGHT + PACKED8 + RMS=1 byte-stream + no PFE crop + BEATS8 burst. Today's config (BPS=FORTY + RMS=0 + PACKED32 + PFE crop + BEATS32) is resolution-agnostic and fixes 480p as a free side-effect of the 720p fixes.

Phase 7a: ✅ solved on first try.

Journal: Phase 7a PASSED — 480p works unchanged on today's pipeline

Pi forced to 720x480p60 via config.txt. Zero firmware changes; capture
auto-reconfigured from TC358743-detected format. Solid-red test: every

sustained. 5/11 row-phase drift gone.

intrinsic to 480p resolution. Today's BPS=FORTY + RMS=0 + PACKED32 +
PFE crop is resolution-agnostic and fixes 480p as a free side-effect.

Phase 7b (297 Mbps) deferred indefinitely — unnecessary. Phase 7c
(Wii through ElectronWarp) remains as isolated test of the
component-to-HDMI chain.

Also: note in capture_pipeline.md that the pipeline is validated at
both 720p60 and 480p60.

EOF
)" && git log --oneline -5

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 22:17:11Z)**_

Committed as `5de2ca6`. Two changes:

**EDID** — VIC 3 and VIC 2 added to the CEA Video Data Block. Preferred/native stays 720p60 (VIC 4), so a Pi without `hdmi_force_hotplug` will negotiate to 720p60 by default; sources that only do 480p (Wii/ElectronWarp) will now find 480p advertised and negotiate there. You can also drop `hdmi_force_hotplug=1` from the Pi config if you want EDID-driven negotiation — or keep it for forcing a specific test mode.

**Probe** — 4 extra lines per frame before the 9-point grid:
```
FIRST (   0,   0) mem: 00 00 FE 00
TopR  ( 719,   0) mem: 00 00 FE 00
BotL  (   0, 479) mem: 00 00 FE 00
LAST  ( 719, 479) mem: 00 00 FE 00
```

If those are clean on next flash, it confirms PFE crop/DMA are writing the exact `[0..W-1] × [0..H-1]` region with no off-by-one on either axis. If any corner shows `55` (sentinel) or mixed, that's the first clue for exactly which edge.

Next flash will test both. Good night.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 22:19:13Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-02 22:19:24Z)**_

Static allocation sized for max 1080p. At [isc_capture.c:17-29](firmware/marvin/default/src/isc_capture.c#L17-L29):

```c
#define ISC_CAP_MAX_W        1920u
#define ISC_CAP_MAX_H        1080u
#define ISC_CAP_BPP          4u
#define ISC_CAP_NUM_BUFFERS  2u

static __attribute__((__section__(".region_cache_aligned")))
       __attribute__((__aligned__(32)))
       uint8_t g_framebuffer[ISC_CAP_MAX_W * ISC_CAP_MAX_H * ISC_CAP_BPP * ISC_CAP_NUM_BUFFERS];
```

One big statically-allocated 1920×1080×4×2 = **15.8 MB** chunk in DDR, 32-byte aligned, in the cached region. Reserved once at link time.

Per-capture, `ISC_Capture_Configure(w,h)` computes `frame_size = w * h * 4` and programs the ISC DMA descriptor for just that span. At 480p: 1.32 MB/frame × 2 = 2.64 MB used out of 15.8 MB. At 720p: 3.69 MB/frame × 2 = 7.37 MB used. At 1080p: 15.8 MB fully used.

**Implications:**

| Resolution | In use | Wasted |
|---|---|---|
| 480p60 | 2.6 MB | 13.2 MB |
| 720p60 | 7.4 MB | 8.4 MB |
| 1080p60 | 15.8 MB | 0 |

Trade-offs:
- **Pro**: resolution can change at runtime (source toggles 480→720) without any re-allocation, fragmentation, or failure modes. Buffer 0/1 base pointers stay constant, simplifying the consumer.
- **Con**: ~13 MB of DDR sits idle at 480p. On a 256 MB (2 Gb DDR3L) Curiosity board, that's ~5% of total DDR — trivial.
- **Con**: no guard page if ISC over-writes (unlikely given PFE crop is hard-bounded). But any resolution change to something larger than 1080p at runtime would silently corrupt whatever's after the buffer. The `width > ISC_CAP_MAX_W || height > ISC_CAP_MAX_H` guard in `ISC_Capture_Configure:141-146` refuses such configs, so that's handled.

Noted in the journal's Open Questions (line 512): *"ISC_Capture framebuffer sized for max 1920×1080 × 2 (~16 MB) — wastes DDR at our current 720×480 use, but trivial at 256 MB total DDR."* So the decision is documented. If DDR ever gets tight (vision working-set + model weights + Legato surfaces), this is the first thing to revisit.

This looks fine — Phase 7c effectively passes. Key reads:

**Pipeline is clean:**
- `WC=2160 rows=480`, full 720×480 captured, 70–71 fps sustained.
- Phase scanner: only 2 transitions across 480 rows (`row 0 → 2`, `row 479 → -1`). **No 5/11 drift.** The historical 480p drift was definitively pipeline-caused, not intrinsic to the Wii/ElectronWarp chain.
- Byte order BGRX32, X=0, all interior b2 values in `C5..CC` range = small analog jitter, expected.

**Peak R ≈ 0xC8 instead of 0xFE — expected for this chain:**
- Pi 720p60 digital → TC358743 limited-range → 0xFE (~99% of 0xEB limited peak).
- Wii → ElectronWarp → TC358743: Wii outputs analog component Y/Pb/Pr; ElectronWarp applies a YPbPr→RGB matrix. 0xC8 ≈ 78% of 0xFF, or 85% of 0xEB limited peak. Loss comes from the component-to-RGB conversion margin + any analog signal attenuation in ElectronWarp.
- The `row=30 rng: b2=[00-D8]` confirms peak red per-row is ~0xD8 (clean center pixels), with 0x00 regions near edges — same story.

**Corners are `00 00 00 00` (black):**
- `row=30 rng: b0=[00-00] b1=[00-00] b2=[00-D8]` — b2 spans all the way to 0 across the row, meaning even mid-vertical rows have black columns somewhere.
- `row 479 → -1` means the last row has no byte ≥ 0x40 in its middle third — that whole row is black.

This is almost certainly **Wii title-safe/action-safe black padding or ElectronWarp letterboxing**. The Wii deliberately outputs black borders in the overscan region because CRTs historically cropped 5-10% of each edge. ElectronWarp may additionally bake in a letterbox. The red "screen" you're displaying isn't reaching pixel (0,0) to (719,479) — it's reaching some inset rectangle. That's content, not a pipeline problem.

**If you want to confirm the extent**, two cheap tests:

1. **Scan inward to find the first non-zero pixel.** Probe at (0,240), (1,240), (2,240), ... until we hit red. That tells us the left-edge black border width. Same for right/top/bottom.
2. **Run a color-bar test pattern instead of solid red.** If the Wii has test patterns (Homebrew or SMG2's debug), the visible bars will map to exact pixel columns.

Or just call it good — you've validated: pipeline works, format is correct, no drift on any source, Wii integrates. The only "question" is the content's active-area geometry, which is a Wii/ElectronWarp property, not ours.
